title: Protocol to Detect and Assess Pollination Deficits in Crops
author: Bernard E. Vaissière
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.pz7dp9n

steps.title: Select and Characterize Study Fields
steps.instruction: Identify study fields growing pollinator-dependent crops in environments with similar topography, soil, slope, and exposure, managed uniformly (same seed source, genetic material, and cropping system).

substeps.instruction: Ensure individual study fields are separated by at least 2 km (or 2-3 km for social bees, up to 6 km for large carpenter bees).
For home gardens, define a 'field' as a set of one or several patches containing the focal crop.
Record field characteristics using Annex 1, including GPS coordinates, altitude, soil type, hedge presence, distance to natural habitat, planting date, density, and variety.

steps.title: Apply Pollination Treatments
steps.instruction: Implement one of the following treatments to modulate pollination levels across the selected fields.

substeps.instruction: Pollinator Supplementation: Introduce managed pollinators (e.g., 1-10 honey bee colonies per ha) at the onset of effective flowering. Use 5 fields with and 5 fields without supplementation. For fields > 450m, introduce pollinators on one side to create a gradient.

Landscape Context: Compare 5 fields in intensive agricultural landscapes vs. 5 fields in landscapes dominated by natural habitats. Alternatively, compare 5 fields close (≤ 200m) and 5 fields far (> 1km) from natural habitat patches (patches should be ≥ 0.5 ha for small bees).
Combined Treatment: Use a factorial design (e.g., 20 fields total) combining both pollinator introduction and landscape context (near/far from natural habitat).
Gradient Design: For fields > 450m, establish a 'pollinator front' (hives or natural area) on one side and set experimental sites at 150m increments (e.g., 25, 175, 325m).

steps.title: Establish Experimental Sites
steps.instruction: Set up data collection areas within each study field based on crop type and field size.

substeps.instruction: For standard herbaceous row crops: Establish a nominal area of 50m x 25m aligned along the rows. In small fields, place in the center; in large fields, place halfway between the center and the edge.
For broadcast-sown crops: Use the same 50m x 25m layout, aligning the long axis with the longest axis of the field.
For orchard crops: Use the tree planting pattern to define the site, ensuring it is large enough to encompass multiple trees.
For home gardens: Use a subset or all available patches of the focal crop.

steps.title: Measure Pollinator Density
steps.instruction: Perform scan sampling of open floral units during the main blooming period (when ≥ 10% of plants are at anthesis) under good weather conditions (temp ≥ 15°C, low wind, no rain, dry vegetation).

substeps.instruction: Establish 4 plots per experimental site. For orchards, a plot is ≥ 2 trees (or 2 of each type if pollenizers are present).
Walk slowly along a set path and record the presence of pollinators on individual floral units (or inflorescences/panicles if flowers are too small/tight).

Scan 100-500 floral units per plot depending on crop: 100 for large flowers (cotton, pumpkin) or low-density crops (French beans, strawberry); 200-250 for apple, cantaloupe, or buckwheat; 400-500 for Brassicaceae (canola, mustard).
Conduct recordings on at least 4 dates during the main flowering period, rotating through 2-4 fixed times per day (e.g., 10:00, 12:00, 14:00, 16:00).
Use two hand counters: one for total floral units observed and one for pollinators seen.

steps.title: Measure Pollinator Diversity
steps.instruction: Collect insect specimens using a sweep net immediately after density recordings under the same weather conditions (temp ≥ 15°C).

substeps.instruction: For herbaceous crops: Capture insects along six 25m long and 2m wide transects, spending 5 minutes per transect (30 mins total per field).
For orchard crops: Capture insects in six plots consisting of pairs of adjacent trees, spending 5 minutes per pair (30 mins total per field).
Kill specimens using potassium cyanide and/or ethyl acetate.
Mount specimens on pins with tags (date, location, crop, collector) or store in a freezer at -20°C or 70% ethanol.
Identify specimens to species level or the taxonomic categories used in density recordings.

steps.title: Collect Covariables
steps.instruction: Record additional variables to explain yield fluctuations and assess plant vigor.

substeps.instruction: Measure flower density (number of floral units at anthesis per unit area) at the same time as pollinator recordings.
For row crops: Use 1m of row (strawberry, cantaloupe) or 3-5m of row (cotton, sunflower).
For broadcast crops: Use a frame of 0.5m² (buckwheat, rape) or 1-2m² (squash).
For orchards: Follow flowering on one or two main branches per tree or use photographs for relative assessment.
Record tree age/trunk diameter and weather conditions.

steps.title: Assess Agronomic and Economic Yield
steps.instruction: Measure the production output using the whole plant as the smallest sampling unit to avoid resource allocation bias.

substeps.instruction: Select a sampling unit: individual plants (best for trees/mixed systems), recording plots (unit length of row or area, best for intermingled crops like buckwheat), or the whole study field.
Harvest produce when fully mature, just before commercial harvest. For perennials, measure over two seasons to account for alternate bearing.
For individual plants/plots, harvest a minimum of 2 plants per plot (trees) or up to 10+ plants (herbaceous determinate crops).
Record agronomic yield: weight (kg) and number of units (fruits/seeds) per m², acre, or ha.
Assess quality: measure average size (diameter, weight), number of filled seeds, or grade (e.g., straightness of runner beans).
Calculate economic yield by multiplying production per unit area by the local producer sale price.

steps.title: Perform Statistical Analysis
steps.instruction: Analyze the relationship between pollination level (independent variable) and yield (dependent variable).

substeps.instruction: For randomized designs with two levels (e.g., with/without pollinators): Use one-way ANOVA.
For factorial designs (e.g., landscape x supplementation): Use two-way ANOVA to test for interaction effects.
For continuous variables (e.g., distance to habitat) or gradient designs: Use regression analysis or ANOVA with contrasts.
Analyze correlations between pollinator density/diversity and yield variables.
